extracted.intended_audience: employers, workers, attorneys, policymakers, and stakeholders interested in federal non-compete rulemaking and enforcement
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards relevant to federal rulemaking, enforcement actions, and public comments concerning post-employment non-compete clauses. Includes definitions, agency positions, treatment of existing agreements, consent-order requirements, and empirical justifications cited by agencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-Compete Clause Rule — unlawful method of competition
rubrics_metrics.description: The Non-Compete Clause Rule provides that it is an unfair method of competition for persons to, among other things, enter into non-compete clauses ("non-competes") with workers on or after the final rule's effective date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied by the Federal Trade Commission as a rulemaking instrument (to be codified at 16 CFR 910). The rulemaking text frames entering into non-competes on or after the effective date as a violation of Section 5 of the FTC Act. See Final and Proposed Rule summaries and codification references in the Federal Register excerpts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of existing non-competes (senior executives exception)
rubrics_metrics.description: With respect to existing non-competes — i.e., non-competes entered into before the effective date — the final rule adopts a different approach for senior executives than for other workers: for senior executives, existing non-competes can remain in force, while existing non-competes with other workers are not enforceable after the effective date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an explicit carve-out in the FTC final rule text; commenters and stakeholders should note the distinction between senior executive treatment and general worker treatment when commenting or assessing compliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a Non-Compete Agreement
rubrics_metrics.description: A Non-Compete Agreement refers to contract terms that, after a worker has ceased working for an employer, restrict the worker's freedom to accept employment with a competing business, to form a competing business, or otherwise to compete with the employer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used in consent agreements and agency analyses to delimit the scope of covered clauses. This formal definition distinguishes non-competes from other post-employment or inter-employer covenants.

rubrics_metrics.name: No-hire provisions are not non-compete clauses
rubrics_metrics.description: No-hire provisions are agreements between two or more employers not to recruit, solicit, or hire each other's employees; they do not fall within the scope of the Commission's failed Non-Compete Clause Rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies (FTC documents) explicitly exclude employer-to-employer no-hire agreements from the definition of employee non-compete clauses; commenters should be careful to distinguish these contract types when drafting or responding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical harms and prevalence evidence for rulemaking
rubrics_metrics.description: Agency materials cite studies finding substantial prevalence of non-competes (e.g., 18–62% in various surveys and cohorts) and empirical findings that non-compete clauses reduce earnings for workers and have broader labor-market effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: FTC, DOL, and other documents invoke empirical studies (with cited percentages and study references) as justification for rulemaking. Commenters can rely on or critique these empirical bases when submitting analyses or economic impact comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Per se unlawful versus reasonableness standard debate
rubrics_metrics.description: Some Commission materials treat non-compete clauses as per se unlawful under Section 5 of the FTC Act, while court decisions (e.g., Seventh Circuit) have held that restrictive non-compete clauses should be subject to a reasonableness assessment regarding duration and scope rather than per se condemnation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This legal framing is central to rule interpretation and litigation risk; commenters should address whether non-competes should be treated per se unlawful or evaluated under a reasonableness/antitrust standard and cite relevant case law and analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consent agreements/consent orders as enforcement tool
rubrics_metrics.description: Consent agreements in FTC matters settle alleged violations of federal law prohibiting unfair methods of competition and often embody terms (consent orders) that prohibit future use of non-compete agreements with certain employees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyses of proposed consent orders describe allegations and the terms of settlement; stakeholders should note what types of non-competes are challenged in settlements and the remedies imposed (e.g., prohibitions, reporting, monitoring).

rubrics_metrics.name: Divestiture-related waivers and personnel protections in DOJ/antitrust orders
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed final judgments and competitive-impact statements require defendants, for Relevant Personnel who elect employment with an acquirer within a specified period (commonly 180 calendar days), to waive all non-compete and non-disclosure agreements and to vest/pay accrued bonuses, incentives, salary, benefits, or other compensation on a prorated basis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a recurring remedy in DOJ antitrust divestiture orders; merger-related comments and compliance plans should address how non-compete waivers and employee transition protections will be handled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency-specific merger/divestiture stance on non-competes (FDIC example)
rubrics_metrics.description: In bank merger reviews, the FDIC states it will generally not view favorably situations where the selling institution enters into non-compete agreements with any employee of the divested entity or seeks to enforce any existing non-compete agreements with those employees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Merger parties should anticipate regulators disfavoring non-competes tied to divestitures and prepare justifications or alternative proposals; commenters may highlight competitive harms in merger remarks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographic/location-dependent exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Some consent agreements and notices reference limited exceptions to non-compete prohibitions that depend on the employee's location of employment (i.e., local-law or location-specific carve-outs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rule and order language may include location-based exceptions; commenters should examine how geographic scope and state law interactions affect enforceability and compliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bargaining context and adequacy of consideration / procedural fairness
rubrics_metrics.description: Enforcement materials note circumstances such as employees not being permitted to negotiate non-compete terms, few employees consulting attorneys, and employees not being offered monetary compensation or job security in exchange for being subject to non-compete restrictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies consider the procedural context (lack of negotiation, unequal bargaining power, absence of consideration) when evaluating the fairness and enforceability of non-competes; commenters should provide facts and analysis about how agreements were presented and bargained-for.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative/regulatory process and small-entity regulatory analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: The FTC's semiannual regulatory agenda and rule notices identify the Non-Compete Clause Rule as to be codified at 16 CFR 910 and note Regulatory Flexibility Act (RFA) considerations and whether the rule is a 'significant regulatory action' with potential impacts on small entities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters should address economic impacts on small entities, state/federal preemption concerns, and regulatory alternatives as part of notice-and-comment submissions; reference docket identifiers and codification citations (e.g., 3084-AB74, 16 CFR 910).
